textbookText: Weismann's Tailless Mice Experiment: Scientist August Weismann conducted a fivegeneration experiment involving 68 white mice, surgically cutting their tails. Surprisingly, no tailless or shorter-tailed mice were born in subsequent generations. Weismann's experiment provided strong evidence against the inheritance of acquired characteristics, especially if changes occurred in somatic cells. However, he proposed the theory of Continuity of germplasm, which implies that heritable traits get transferred through germ cells in the ovaries and testicles.

Neo-Lamarckism emerged as a response, reevaluating the theory. Recent research highlighted that body traits result from interactions between hereditary factors and environmental conditions that influence evolution. According to the germplasm theory, organisms have two types of cells – i.somatic cell (somatoplasm) ii.germinal cells (germplasm) Only changes that happen in the germinal cells can be passed down to offspring. This means that if something changes in the somatic cells, like the body cells, it usually won't be passed on to the next generation.

7.3.3 DARWINISM (Theory of Natural Selection) Darwinism is a theory of organic evolution propounded by Charles Darwin as an explanation of changes in living beings that is driven mainly by natural selection. Darwin's meticulous research and observations, primarily conducted during his journey aboard HMS Beagle from 1831 to 1836, laid the foundation of this theory in the field of modern evolutionary biology. Exploring diverse regions like the Galápagos Islands, South America, and Australia, the systematic arrangement of flora, fauna, and geological formations, shaped his later discoveries. Darwinism is based on several facts and observations. The five fundamental facts are:

a. Enormous fertility b. Struggle for existence c. Variation and heredity d. Natural selection e. Origin of species a) Enormous fertility: All living things have an extraordinary ability to reproduce in

geometric ratio. This type of reproductive potential can be observed in nature in various organisms: i. An oyster lays around 80 million eggs in a year. ii. A starfish produces about a million eggs every season. If all of them survive and continue to reproduce, a single species will fill all the sea after a few generations. iii. Paramecium divides three times within 48 hours. iv. A salmon produces 28 million eggs in a single breeding season. v. A slow breeding elephant couple, in 800 years, can give 29 million offsprings. b) Struggle for existence: Darwin observed three types of struggle for existence: i. Intraspecific struggle: This is the struggle between individuals of the same species for food, shelter, breeding place, etc. For instance, dogs compete with one another for flesh. ii. Interspecific struggle: This is the struggle between individuals of different species. For example, both leopards and wolves hunt rabbits. Elephants, rhinos and deer sometimes wander into farmland nearby national parks for food, which can cause problems for farmers. At the same time, people clear forests to make space for farms, which affects the habitat of these animals. This competition for land and food shows how humans and wildlife struggle for survival. iii. Environmental struggle: This is the struggle against environmental challenges like floods, droughts, cold and other natural disasters.
